newsitem.title: USA: Talks continue in GM's Indiana truck strike.
newsitem.headline: Talks continue in GM's Indiana truck strike.

text.p: Talks to resolve a five-day-old strike at a General Motors Corp. pickup truck plant continued Tuesday but union officials indicated progress was slow.

About 2,700 members of United Auto Workers Local 2209 walked off the job at the Fort Wayne, Ind., plant on Friday after the two sides failed to reach agreement on contract terms by the strike deadline.

The union wants GM to address health and safety issues and add more jobs to cut down on overtime. GM, which would like to shed 30,000 hourly U.S. workers over the next three years through attrition, has thus far balked at the UAW's demands.
Company and union bargainers resumed talks early Tuesday after working until 6 p.m. EST on Monday, GM spokesman Daniel Flores said. He decined to characterise the discussions.
"Obviously we're encouraged that both sides are meeting and the talks are continuing," he said.
Union officials said that progress in the talks was slow.

Although dealers have ample inventories of Chevrolet C/K and GMC Sierra pickup trucks, Burnham Securities Inc. analyst David Healy said GM may decide to settle the dispute within a week or two before losing too much more production.

"I would think it's likely to be settled sooner rather than later," he said. "To me, it looks like one of those things the company could give a little bit on without setting a precedent for the other (locals) that are still hanging."
GM is still working to reach agreements with about 40 percent of its 105 UAW locals. Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp. are both much closer to wrapping up all of their local agreements.
Last November, Detroit's Big Three automakers reached a new national agreement with the UAW, which acts as a framework for settling local pacts.
The talks at the Fort Wayne plant are being watched closely since it is the first union local where a strike has erupted since the national agreement was signed.
The Fort Wayne plant makes about 5,500 regular cab C/K and Sierra pickup trucks a week.
Healy at Burnham Securities estimates GM would lose profits of about $25 million a week from the strike. However, he said the automaker could make up some of that production in the second quarter.
